tldr: This paper shows that for humanoid text-to-motion, you don't need any extra training. By simply sampling multiple candidates from a frozen generator and picking the best one using the real deployment controller rolled out in simulation, you can push hardware success rates right up to the theoretical ceiling (89.5%).
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed S³ (Sample, Simulate, Select) pipeline. Human skeletal motions generated by a frozen text-to-motion model (left) are retargeted to robot joint references via direction-matching IK (center). They are then rolled out in simulation using the deployment tracking policy (right) to select the best motion for real-world execution.
overview:
Having a humanoid robot move just by telling it "walk forward and wave" sounds ideal. But there is a major roadblock. Text-to-motion models are trained on human data, so they know nothing about robot dynamics like mass or joint torque limits. Meanwhile, whole-body tracking controllers on the robot reliably execute reference motions, but they cannot replan if fed an infeasible trajectory.

Recent works try to bridge this gap by collecting robot joint data to train dedicated models, or by fine-tuning with simulator feedback. But that raises a simple question: how far can you actually get just by combining existing generators and controllers without any training? Prior works claiming gains from training never measured this baseline.

To find out, the authors built S³ (Sample, Simulate, Select), an extremely simple training-free pipeline. It samples 8 motions per prompt, retargets them to a Unitree G1 via direction-matching inverse kinematics (IK), and rolls them out in a physics simulator using the actual deployment controller (SONIC). It then simply picks the candidate that stayed upright and tracked best.

Across extensive benchmarks, selecting from just 8 candidates boosted upright success from 80.5% to 89.5%, and hardware-gate passes jumped by 2.6x. When executed on a physical G1 across 177 distinct motions, the robot completed every single clip standing without falling once. It is a satisfying paper showing that instead of rushing to train new models, putting a physics simulator in a selection loop solves most of the problem.
contributions: Introducing S³, a physics-in-the-loop text-to-motion pipeline that requires zero training and uses the deployment policy's physics simulation directly as a verifier.
Validating physical feasibility and success rates at an unprecedented scale across the entire HumanML3D test set (4,184 prompts) and on a physical Unitree G1 (177 motions).
Quantitatively demonstrating that kinematic fall predictors struggle to rank candidates for the same prompt, making full physics rollouts essential as a verifier.
Pinpointing the fundamental limit that training-free selection cannot fix down to a single class: prompts that lower the pelvis (such as squatting and sitting).

sections.heading: How Far Can You Go Without Training? Turning the Deployment Controller into a Verifier
sections.summary: This work tests how much of the physical gap between text-to-motion and humanoid tracking can be closed without extra training, simply by sampling multiple motions and picking the best one in simulation. Using a deterministic simulator as the verifier allows directly measuring the theoretical any-of-N ceiling.
sections.details:
Both human text-to-motion models and RL-based humanoid tracking controllers have advanced rapidly in recent years. Yet there is a severe dynamics gap between them. Human motion generators ignore robot mass distribution, joint limits, and contact patterns, while tracking controllers fall over when fed physically infeasible references.

Prior work closed this gap by training models on robot data or fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. However, no one had measured how far you can get with an off-the-shelf, training-free baseline combining existing models.

The authors' insight is simple: the deployment controller itself is the best judge of feasibility. Fast modern tracking controllers (like SONIC) take only about 3 seconds of CPU time on a single core to roll out a 5-second clip in MuJoCo, while generator (MoMask) inference takes around 1 second. Why not sample multiple motions per prompt, roll them all out in physics simulation, and send the best-tracked one to hardware? This paper sets out to reveal that zero-training ceiling.

captions.F1: A physical Unitree G1 executing motions using a frozen text-to-motion model and a pretrained controller with zero additional training. In a single run, the robot stably walks while waving its hand.

sections.heading: Where Text-to-Motion Meets Robot Tracking: How This Differs from Prior Work
sections.summary: The paper reviews human text-to-motion, robot retargeting and tracking, and recent language-to-humanoid systems. While prior methods train robot-specific models or fine-tune them, this work keeps components completely frozen, selects via a physics loop, and evaluates at an unprecedented scale.
sections.details:
### Human-Space Text-to-Motion
Following the HumanML3D benchmark, diffusion models and token-based autoregressive models (like MoMask) have advanced rapidly. However, these rely on the SMPL human skeleton and ignore contact forces, balance, and actuator torque limits.

### Humanoid Retargeting and Tracking
Retargeting techniques that map human motion to robot joints (like GMR) and tracking policies that follow them on hardware (like HOVER and SONIC) have matured. In particular, this work uses SONIC, a general-purpose tracking foundation model pretrained on over 100 million frames of motion capture data.

### Prior Language-to-Humanoid Systems
Prior works generally fall into three camps: (1) retraining generative models in robot joint space (UH-1, TEXEDO), (2) end-to-end models predicting control inputs directly from language (LangWBC), and (3) fine-tuning human-space generators with rewards from physics simulators (RLPF).

The closest prior work, TEXEDO, generates 32 candidates and ranks them using a lightweight verifier trained to imitate SONIC before hardware execution. In contrast, this paper uses the deterministic simulator itself as the verifier, without retraining the generator. Furthermore, while TEXEDO tested 30 prompts and UH-1 tested 12 on hardware, this study conducts an exhaustive evaluation across 177 real-world prompts and 4,184 simulation prompts.

sections.heading: S³ (Sample, Simulate, Select): Zero-Training Physics-in-the-Loop
sections.summary: MoMask samples $N$ motions from a prompt, direction-matching IK retargets them to the G1, and the deployment policy SONIC rolls them out in MuJoCo to pick the best. The authors carefully design fall detection rules, a hardware safety gate, and an evaluation protocol that preserves semantic fidelity.
sections.details:
### III-A Overview and Formulation
Given a prompt $p$, a frozen generator $G$ samples $N$ human joint trajectories. A retargeter $R$ converts each into joint and floating-base references for the G1, and the deployment policy $\pi$ executes them in simulation. From the rollout, safety gate status and tracking errors are computed, and the best candidate is selected lexicographically.

### III-B Sample: Frozen Text-to-Motion
The pipeline uses MoMask pretrained on HumanML3D out of the box, generating $N$ 22-joint trajectories at 20 fps per prompt. No spatial scaling is applied, except for ground-plane contact adjustment.

### III-C Retarget: Direction-Matching IK
Matching human bone lengths directly to a robot causes unnatural poses, so the authors use direction-matching inverse kinematics (IK) that preserves limb direction vectors. After constructing a target skeleton with robot segment lengths, damped least squares solves for G1 joint angles, which are resampled to 50 Hz. Across the AMASS dataset, limb orientation error is only $4.2^{\circ}$.

### III-D Simulate: Deployment Policy as the Verifier
NVIDIA's SONIC policy (in ONNX format), intended for the physical robot, runs directly in MuJoCo (50 Hz control, 200 Hz physics).
- Fall detection: Relying solely on absolute pelvis height would incorrectly classify squats as falls. A fall is defined as: (1) pelvis height below 0.25 m, (2) torso tilt exceeding 60 degrees, or (3) pelvis dipping >0.30 m below the reference for over 0.5 seconds.
- Safety gate: Rollouts are classified as REJECT (fell), CAUTION (excessive initial velocity or joint velocity), or PASS (safe).

### III-E Select and Baselines
The candidate with the best gate status and lowest tracking error is selected. Comparisons include "Single" (first sample), "Kinematic best-of-N" (predicting falls from generator outputs), and "Oracle" (theoretical ceiling where any success among $N$ counts).

### III-F & III-G Semantic Fidelity and Hardware Deployment
To ensure selection does not just favor static, trivial motions, semantic alignment is tracked using standard HumanML3D evaluators (R-precision, Matching score). For real-world execution, clips are bookended with 3-second and 2-second cosine blends for safe transitions, running sequentially in 8-clip sessions.

sections.heading: What 4,000+ Simulations and 177 Real-World Trials Revealed: Ceilings and Limits
sections.summary: Sampling just 8 candidates raised upright execution from 80.5% to 89.5% and boosted hardware-gate passes by 2.6x. Kinematic predictors could not rank intra-prompt candidates, proving physics simulation is essential, while the sole failure mode localized to pelvis-lowering motions.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Main Results: What Selection Achieves
Across 200 stratified HumanML3D test prompts (locomotion, turns, upper-body, squat/bend, jump, etc.), Single upright execution was 83.5% (33 PASS), while S³ with $N=8$ reached 89.5% (85 PASS, a 2.6x increase). On the full 4,184-prompt test split, upright execution similarly rose from 80.5% to 89.5% (PASS jumped from 704 to 1,680). Most gains were achieved by $N=4$, plateauing near $N=7$.

### Comparison with Robot-Space Trained TEXEDO
When evaluating TEXEDO's robot-trained generator under the same verifier, Single achieved 97.0% and best-of-8 reached 98.0%. Training on robot data offers clear value that selection alone cannot match by fundamentally resolving squatting motions.

### IV-C Why Kinematic Predictors Fall Short
A classifier trained on geometric features (like torso tilt) predicts falls with a high AUROC of 0.90. However, using it to rank 8 candidates only brings success to 85.0%. While it can separate easy from hard motions across the population, ranking 8 subtle variations from the same prompt requires rolling out full physics.

### IV-D The Boundary of Selection: Lowering the Pelvis
By category, locomotion (98%), upper-body (92%), and jumps (95%) performed almost flawlessly. In contrast, "squat/bend" only improved from 50% to 57%. Nearly all unrecovered prompts involved lowering the pelvis, like sitting in a chair or picking something off the floor. The generator outputs deep human-scale squats that violate center-of-mass balance on the robot's shorter legs.

### IV-E Semantic Degradation and Retargeting Ablation
Evaluating semantic fidelity showed that scores drop noticeably once motions are projected onto the robot's morphology. However, real mocap data projected onto the robot suffered the exact same drop, confirming this is an unavoidable morphological floor rather than generator error. Furthermore, combining direction-matching IK with optimization-based retargeting (GMR) produced complementary fixes, pushing the any-of-8 ceiling to 95.0%.

### IV-G Real-World Verification on Unitree G1
All 177 gate-selected clips were deployed on a physical G1, and all 177 completed while remaining upright (100% success rate). Joint tracking errors between simulation and hardware correlated exceptionally well ($r=0.94$), confirming that MuJoCo rollouts reliably predict real-world execution.

sections.heading: Key Takeaways and Open Questions: The Boundary Between Training and Selection
sections.summary: Simulation-based selection multiplies hardware-executable clips by 2.6x for just a few CPU seconds, but it cannot create motions the generator never produces. The authors discuss the benefits of human-space generation and the limitations of open-loop control without environmental perception.
sections.details:
### Scope and Limits of Rollout-Based Selection
Simulating deployment policies allows filtering for hardware-executable motions with a 2.6x yield improvement at negligible cost (a few CPU seconds per candidate). However, selection cannot materialize motions that the generator fundamentally cannot produce. While training on robot data (like TEXEDO) shifts the base distribution of valid motions (resolving squats), selection picks the best existing candidate. The two approaches are complementary rather than conflicting.

### Why Keep Generation in Human Space?
Training models directly in robot joint space means retraining from scratch whenever the robot embodiment changes. In contrast, keeping generation in human space and retargeting allows porting to different humanoids simply by modifying kinematic link definitions.

### Limitations and Future Outlook
The current pipeline operates offline and open-loop. It also lacks environmental sensing, assuming a flat, empty plane. If a prompt says "sit on a chair" or "climb stairs," the absence of physical chairs or stairs causes balance failures, which accounts for many pelvis-lowering issues. Future extensions include streaming pipelines and integrating scene perception.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Run the Simulator First! A New Benchmark from a Training-Free Baseline
sections.summary: Sampling multiple candidates from a frozen text-to-motion model and selecting via simulated deployment rollouts achieved an 89.5% success rate across 4,184 prompts, with all 177 hardware trials remaining upright. This zero-training ceiling and its identified failure modes provide the true baseline for future language-to-humanoid research.
sections.details:
This study introduced and evaluated S³, connecting a frozen text-to-motion model with a pretrained tracking policy via physics simulation without any additional training.

Upright execution rose from 80.5% to 89.5% across the full HumanML3D test set, and 177 motions tested on the physical Unitree G1 ran with zero falls (100% completion). The experiments demonstrated that kinematic statistical predictors cannot reliably rank intra-prompt candidates, proving the necessity of putting full physics simulation in the loop.

The sole unresolved failure mode was motions that lower the pelvis, marking the exact boundary where retraining on robot data becomes necessary. Any future work proposing new language-to-motion models for humanoids should be measured against how much it actually improves upon this training-free simulation-selection baseline.

takeaways: Before jumping into complex fine-tuning or retraining, try a best-of-N selection using a lightweight physics simulator (like MuJoCo) as a verifier.
Even if a kinematic metric predicts falls well across a dataset (AUROC 0.90), it fails to rank subtle variations from the same prompt; rolling out actual physical dynamics is essential.
The biggest vulnerability of a human-space generator + retargeter pipeline is pelvis-lowering motions (squatting, sitting), which is the only category truly requiring robot-data retraining.
When the simulator and deployment policy are properly matched, simulation tracking error correlates strongly with real-world error ($r=0.94$), virtually eliminating hardware damage risks.
limitations: Motions that the generator fundamentally cannot produce (such as deep squats incompatible with robot limb proportions) cannot be recovered no matter how many samples are drawn.
Lacking environmental sensing or object interaction, prompts that assume a chair or steps will always miss their targets and cause the robot to lose balance.
Because it operates as an entirely offline, open-loop batch pipeline, it cannot handle real-time instruction changes or dynamic trajectory replanning under disturbances.
